rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Dimensional analysis expresses every physical quantity as a product of powers of base dimensions (M, L, T, ...). rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Force: $[F] = [MLT^{-2}]$
Work/Energy/Torque: $[ML^2T^{-2}]$
Power: $[ML^2T^{-3}]$; Pressure/Stress/Energy density: $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Homogeneity Constraint:** Only quantities with the same dimensional formula can be added, subtracted, or equated in an equation. Term-by-term analysis is mandatory.  ·  **Function Argument Constraint:** The arguments of trigonometric (e.g., sin θ, cos θ), exponential (e.g., $e^x$), and logarithmic functions must be dimensionless. This is a critical check for determining the dimensions of unknown constants in an equation.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: Memorise the standard table — NEB asks dimensional formulas of force, momentum, power, pressure, G, h, viscosity and surface tension nearly every year.  ·  Note 2: In derivation questions, ALWAYS begin by writing the assumed product-of-powers form and end by interpreting the exponents.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Example 1: Check $s = ut + \ frac{1}{2}at^2$: $[LT^{-1}][T] + [LT^{-2}][T^2] = [L] + [L] = [L]$ ✓ — both terms are lengths, matching the LHS.  ·  Example 2: A sphere of radius $r$ moving slowly with speed $v$ through a fluid of viscosity $\eta$ experiences drag $F = k\,\eta^a r^b v^c$ (Stokes' law). Matching $[MLT^{-2}] = [ML^{-1}T^{-1}]^a [L]^b [LT^{-1}]^c$ gives $a = 1$, $b = 1$, $c = 1$ → $F = 6\pi\eta r v$.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'If an equation is dimensionally correct, it is physically correct.' ✅ Homogeneity is a necessary but not sufficient test — $T = \sqrt{l/g}$ and $T = 3\sqrt{l/g}$ are both dimensionally correct; only one is true (the constant $2\pi$ is invisible to dimensions).  ·  ❌ 'Dimensional formula and dimensional equation are the same.' ✅ The formula is $[F] = [MLT^{-2}]$; the equation is $F = [MLT^{-2}]$ — the equation shows the quantity equated to its dimensions.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Prepare a memorised table of 15 standard dimensional formulas (force → luminous flux).  ·  Task 2: Derive $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, $v = \sqrt{F/\mu}$ and $F = 6\pi\eta rv$ fully by the powers method.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Build dimensional formulas from known definitions rather than memorising: force = ma, then chain (power = F·v, pressure = F/A, etc.).  ·  Trick 2: 'Same dimensions' pairs frequently asked: work–torque–energy; Planck's constant–angular momentum; impulse–momentum; pressure–energy density; gravitational potential–velocity squared.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Define dimensional formula and dimensional equation with one example each.  ·  Q2. State the principle of homogeneity of dimensions and use it to test the equation $v = u - at$.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 1: A 2-mark derivation by the powers method (pendulum, string wave, Stokes' law) appears in NEB almost every year — practise the full written format.  ·  Exam Tip 2: Always state limitations when asked to 'derive and comment' — omitting them costs the last mark.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Concept 1: Base quantities (M, L, T, I, Θ, J, N) and derived quantities expressed as dimensional formulas.  ·  Concept 2: Principle of homogeneity — the fundamental test of dimensional validity of any equation.  ·  Concept 3: Method of powers for deriving relations: assume product form, equate exponents per base dimension.  ·  Concept 4: Unit conversion via dimensional formula: n₂ = n₁ × (scale factors)^(exponents).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Dimensional homogeneity is a necessary test of correctness — it can reject an equation but can never fully prove one.  ·  Dimensionless constants (½, 2π, e) are invisible to dimensional analysis.  ·  Quantities with identical dimensions can still be physically different (work vs torque; energy vs moment).  ·  The powers method can only solve for as many unknown exponents as there are independent base dimensions (usually 3: M, L, T).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Dimensional analysis was pioneered by Fourier (1822) and developed into a systematic tool by Rayleigh; the Buckingham π theorem is its formal generalisation used throughout engineering.  ·  The 2019 SI redefinition fixed $h$ (Planck constant), $c$, $e$, $k_B$, $N_A$ etc. exactly — every unit is now dimensionally anchored to fundamental constants.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. Assuming the period $T$ of a simple pendulum depends on its length $l$ and acceleration due to gravity $g$, derive the relation $T = k\sqrt{l/g}$ dimensionally.  ·  Q4. Convert 1 newton into dyne using dimensional analysis.  ·  Q5. Write three limitations of dimensional analysis.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 3: For conversion numericals, show $n_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2$ explicitly; the final factor without working earns half marks only.  ·  Exam Tip 4: Check answers dimensionally at the end of every long derivation — it takes 30 seconds and catches most slips.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Example 3: Convert a pressure of 1 pascal into CGS units: $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$ → $1 \ imes 1000 \ imes 10^{-2} = 10$ dyn cm⁻² = 10 barye.  ·  Example 4: The energy $E$ of a photon is $hf$; verify: $h[ML^2T^{-1}] \ imes f[T^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$ = dimensions of energy ✓.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The dimensional formula of coefficient of viscosity is: → A  ·  Which pair has the SAME dimensions? → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Dimensional formula** expresses a physical quantity in terms of the seven base quantities using symbols M (mass), L (length), T (time), I (current), Θ (temperature), J (luminous intensity) and N (amount of substance). Examples: velocity $[M^0 L^1 T^{-1}]$, force $[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]$, energy $[M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]$, pressure $[M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.  ·  **Principle of homogeneity:** a physically correct equation must have identical dimensions in every term. You can add 3 apples to 4 apples but not 3 apples to 4 metres — likewise $v = u + at$ works because every term is a velocity $[LT^{-1}]$.  ·  **Use 1 — checking equations:** replace every quantity by its dimensional formula and verify the two sides match. If they don't, the equation is certainly wrong. If they do match, the equation is *probably* right (never proof — a factor of ½ is dimensionless and invisible).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Dimensionless quantities (strain, angle, refractive index) and their special role in functional arguments.  ·  Gravitational constant: $[G] = [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$; Planck constant: $[h] = [ML^2T^{-1}]$  ·  Unit conversion: $n_2 = n_1 \left(\ rac{M_1}{M_2}\ ight)^a\left(\ rac{L_1}{L_2}\ ight)^b\left(\ rac{T_1}{T_2}\ ight)^c$ for $[M^aL^bT^c]$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Dimensionless Constant Constraint:** Dimensional analysis inherently cannot identify or verify dimensionless constants (e.g., $2\pi$, 0.5). These factors must be determined via independent theoretical derivation or experimental calibration.  ·  Angle (radian) and steradian are supplementary, dimensionless $[M^0L^0T^0]$ units.  ·  Any term inside sin, cos, exp, log must be dimensionless.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Angle has units but no dimensions, so it is not a physical quantity.' ✅ Angle is a dimensionless $[M^0L^0T^0]$ SUPPLEMENTARY quantity — it has a unit (radian) but zero exponents in M, L, T.  ·  ❌ 'Trigonometric, exponential and log functions can be applied to dimensional quantities.' ✅ Their arguments MUST be dimensionless — $\sin(\omega t)$ is valid only because $\omega t$ is an angle (dimensionless).  ·  ❌ '1 newton = 1 dyn.' ✅ $1\,\ ext{N} = 10^5\,\ ext{dyn}$ — dimensional conversion ($[MLT^{-2}]$: 1000 g × 100 cm) gives the factor $10^5$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Dimensional analysis can determine the scalar/vector nature of a quantity.' ✅ It cannot — work and torque have identical dimensions $[ML^2T^{-2}]$ yet work is scalar, torque is vector.  ·  Example 5: Find dimensions of $\ rac{a}{b}$ in $P = \ rac{a - b t^2}{x}$, where P = pressure, x = distance, t = time. Numerator must be $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}][L] = [MT^{-2}]$; so $[a] = [MT^{-2}]$ and $[b] = [MT^{-4}]$ → $\ rac{a}{b} = [T^2]$.  ·  Note 3: When converting units, keep the dimensional exponents of the QUANTITY (not of the units) — the commonest source of sign errors.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Note 4: Dimensionless groups (Reynolds number, Mach number) are the basis of scale-model testing in engineering — same dimensions in, same physics out.  ·  Note 1: Work and torque share dimensions $[ML^2T^{-2}]$ but differ physically (scalar vs vector) — dimensions do not define a quantity.  ·  Note 2: The pendulum derivation gives $T = k\sqrt{l/g}$; the constant $k = 2\pi$ must come from experiment or full theory.
